memory_candidates.content: To measure deploy-tree orphan files (deployed but no longer declared in the source store) reliably, do NOT diff the live tree against the source manifest by inspection. Instead: git clone the repo into a scratch directory (inherits the active-extension state file but starts with no deploy tree at all), run the project's headless deploy script against that scratch path to get a genuine clean regenerate, then diff live-vs-scratch file listings. Filter the raw diff for non-manifest runtime noise before trusting it: session-lock/tmp files, uncommitted working-tree artifacts (a scratch clone only pulls committed content), and any path explicitly listed in a syncprotect file (those are legitimately excluded from overwrite, not orphans).

A task description's own 'REVISED' scope-correction note is not self-verifying evidence -- it can itself be wrong, especially when a prior staleness caveat means the correction may have been produced under the same conditions (a stale tree, or an eyeballed directory listing instead of an actual declared-vs-deployed diff) that necessitated the caveat in the first place. Always independently re-run the measurement a revision claims to have taken before treating its corrected numbers as authoritative, rather than assuming a later-dated note supersedes an earlier one by recency alone.

When verifying parity between a source-of-truth store and a generated/deployed tree that is fanned in from MANY owners (multiple extensions, packages, or plugins all copying into one target directory), the reverse direction -- finding deployed files no longer declared by anything -- must be computed as a WHOLE-TREE operation over the union of all owners' declared sets, never per-owner. A per-owner subtractive check is wrong by construction: owner A's undeclared file is routinely owner B's declared file, so every per-owner pass reports the other owners' legitimate content as orphans. The forward direction (declared-but-missing, hash mismatch) is safely per-owner, which is why codebases naturally grow the forward check per-owner and then find the reverse check does not fit the same loop. Build the reverse check as a separate whole-tree entry point that reuses the same declared-side enumeration primitive, and pair it with an explicit, named exclusion contract for legitimately-undeclared content (runtime artifacts, merged/generated files, protected paths) -- without that contract the check produces constant false positives and is ignored.
